summary:
Yukon stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-motivation provisions, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodation is prohibited in Yukon as in all provinces and territories, with gender identity and expression explicitly listed as prohibited grounds in all Canadian human rights statutes as of 2017. Section 15(1) Charter equality concepts of sex and physical disability have been interpreted to include transsexuality, applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement; claims against private businesses proceed under the applicable human rights statutes interpreted consistently with Charter values.

Legal gender recognition is available in Yukon. Vital statistics and identity documents such as birth certificates fall under territorial jurisdiction, and transgender people can change their legal gender under varying territorial rules.

National hate-crime data shows a rising pattern for trans-motivated incidents. Statistics Canada's release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024' (30 March 2026) reports 4,882 police-reported hate crimes in 2024, up 1% on 2023 and 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents targeting gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive yearly increase and up 184% since 2020. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, though June 2024 alone recorded 113 incidents against a monthly average near 50. Police-reported hate-crime rates run about 2.5 times higher in large metropolitan areas (13.9 per 100,000) than in smaller towns (5.5), a gap that bears on sparsely populated territories where reporting infrastructure is thinner. Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis examines the same national data and does not report Yukon-level victimisation.

Yukon's own legislature has placed trans residents on cross-party record. On 30 March 2026 the Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility, with Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko (Kluane) praising the courage, resilience and contributions of transgender, two-spirited and gender-diverse Yukoners, acknowledging that too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment and hate for far too long, and citing a national study showing transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of a suicide attempt.

Official hostility toward trans-inclusive school policy has been met with ministerial defence. In June 2024 a Pride flag was allegedly vandalized and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in Whitehorse's Porter Creek neighbourhood; a replacement was promptly put up, and on 12 June 2024 Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy (SOGI 123).

Canada in 2022 became the third country and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults, making it a Criminal Code offence. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for institutional bias and pledged to stand against transphobia through an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee.

Sub-national policy turbulence in schools and sport is concentrated in other provinces, not Yukon: Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 using a gender-related preferred name or gender identity, and Alberta's 2024 Health Statutes Amendment Act, Education Amendment Act and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act were shielded from legal challenge by Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause.

Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on 27 June 1969. Since June 2019 the general age of consent is 16, rising to 18 where a relationship of trust, authority or dependency exists, with limited close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. Criminal Code section 159 on anal intercourse was repealed by Bill C-75, which received royal assent 21 June 2019; assented 21 June 2019, S.C. 2019, c. 25, the repeal applies in Yukon and bars conviction for any historical sexual offence unless the act would constitute an offence if committed on the day the charge was laid.

In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 Charter equality as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15. Same-sex marriage was legalized nationwide on 20 July 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, the first country to do so without a residency requirement. Adoption by same-sex couples was legalized in Yukon in 2003, part of nationwide legalization completed by Nunavut in 2011. On 21 June 2018 royal assent to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allows persons convicted of certain homosexual acts before 1969 or anal intercourse under repealed section 159 to have records destroyed, following the 28 November 2017 prime ministerial apology.

In a 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office, 87.6% said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person, against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual next-door neighbour.

Many transgender people in traditional Indigenous roles held positions of reverence as caretakers of children who had lost families, spiritual healers and warriors in battle, with distinct terms such as Cree napew iskwewisêhot and iskwew ka napewayat, Ktunaxa titqattek, Blackfoot aakii'skassi, Inuit sipiniq, and Ojibwe ikwekaazo and ininiikaazo. Those traditions declined after colonisation and the spread of Christianity with forced assimilation; in the early 1990s Indigenous LGBTQ groups proposed "two-spirit" to reclaim a traditional cultural third gender, now frequently used in LGBT2S and LGBTQ2S designations.
tangentialFactors:
Police-reported hate-crime rates are roughly 2.5 times higher in large metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, a distribution that cuts against assuming sparsely populated Yukon is insulated from hate crime; reporting infrastructure in small jurisdictions is thinner, so low territorial counts may reflect under-reporting rather than lower incidence.

The Statistics Canada release breaks out gender identity or expression and sexual orientation as separate motivation categories, so trans-specific hate-crime volume is measurable nationally but not at Yukon level; Egale Canada's analysis likewise reports national figures only.

Sub-national policy turbulence in Canadian schools and sport is concentrated in Saskatchewan and Alberta, both of which used the notwithstanding clause; Yukon's legislature moved in the opposite direction with its March 2026 cross-party tribute, and Yukon's education minister publicly defended the territory's SOGI 123 policy after a Pride flag was stolen from a Whitehorse school.

A 2020 Privy Council Office poll found 87.6% comfortable having a transgender neighbour against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour, a narrow gap on the headline measure of social acceptance.

outOfScopeNotes:
